clean_story:
User needs. Design for them.

The term UX Design comes from User Experience Design, meaning shaping how people feel when using a product. A door handle suggests push or pull without words. A website guides your eyes to the right button before you realize it. Good UX feels invisible, like a well-oiled hinge. Bad UX feels like a door that only opens if you kick it just right.

In 1993, Don Norman at Apple coined the term to describe his work making computers less frustrating. He noticed people blamed themselves for mistakes, not the confusing design. His solution? Study how humans think, then build tools that match. Today, UX designers map user journeys like cartographers, marking pain points and smooth paths. A banking app hides complex steps behind one tap. A game controller fits hands after years of ergonomic tweaks.

Precision matters. Amazon found every 100 milliseconds of load time cost 1 percent in sales. A single misplaced button can make a difference between a sale and a bounce.

Three related subjects are human psychology, interface simplicity and product usability.
